modules.title: Syntax Basics, Variables & Data Types

pages.title: Anatomy of a C Program
pages.markdown:
## Where Execution Begins

Every C program has exactly one entry point: `int main(void)`. When you run a compiled program, the operating system loads it and jumps to `main` — nothing runs before that except C runtime startup code that sets up the stack and calls constructors for global objects (there mostly aren't any in plain C).

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("Hello, world!\n");
    return 0;
}
```

The `return 0;` at the end is the program's **exit status**, handed back to the shell. By convention `0` means success and any nonzero value signals an error — `echo $?` on a Unix shell shows you the last exit code.

## The Preprocessor Runs First

`#include <stdio.h>` is not a normal statement — it's a **preprocessor directive**, processed in a separate text-substitution pass before the compiler ever sees your code. The preprocessor literally pastes the contents of `stdio.h` (declarations for `printf`, `scanf`, `FILE`, etc.) into your source file. This two-stage model — preprocess, then compile — is unique to C's heritage and still shapes how large C programs are organized into headers (`.h`) and source files (`.c`).

## Declaring Variables

C is **statically typed**: every variable's type is fixed at compile time and never changes.

```c
int age = 36;        // whole number
double height = 1.7; // double-precision floating point
char grade = 'A';    // a single character (really a small integer)
float weight = 68.5f; // single-precision floating point
```

Unlike dynamically typed languages, you cannot later assign a string to `age` — the compiler rejects type mismatches (with warnings, sometimes errors, depending on how incompatible the types are).

## Printing Values

`printf` doesn't know the types of its arguments at compile time — it relies on you supplying a matching **format specifier** for each one:

- `%d` — `int`
- `%f` — `float`/`double` (as an argument to `printf`, `float` is promoted to `double`)
- `%c` — `char`
- `%s` — a null-terminated string (`char*`)
- `%.1f` — a `double` with one digit after the decimal point

```c
printf("Age: %d, Height: %.1f, Grade: %c\n", age, height, grade);
```

Getting a specifier wrong (e.g. `%d` for a `double`) is **undefined behavior** — it may print garbage, crash, or happen to "work," because `printf` trusts you and reads its variadic arguments based purely on the format string.

## Recap

A C program starts at `main`, returns an integer exit status, and pulls in library declarations via `#include`. Every variable has a fixed, explicit type, and `printf`/format-specifier pairs must match exactly — there's no runtime type checking to save you.

pages.title: Memory Layout of Basic Types
Idioms, Naming & Common Pitfalls
pages.markdown:
## Prefer Initialization at Declaration

Idiomatic C initializes variables where they're declared whenever a sensible starting value exists:

```c
int count = 0;
double total = 0.0;
char initial = '\0';
```

This avoids an entire class of "used before set" bugs and makes code easier to reason about — you never wonder whether a variable might still hold garbage at the point you read it.

## Choosing the Right Type

- Use `int` for ordinary whole numbers/counters (it's the "natural" word size the CPU handles fastest).
- Use `size_t` (unsigned) for sizes, lengths, and array indices — it's what `sizeof` and standard library functions like `strlen` return, and it's guaranteed wide enough to represent the size of any object.
- Use `double` over `float` by default for floating point — `float`'s reduced precision accumulates error quickly, and `double` is what all the `<math.h>` functions expect.
- Reach for `<stdint.h>`'s `int32_t`/`uint8_t`/etc. when the exact bit width genuinely matters (binary file formats, network packets, hardware registers).

## `const` Signals Intent

`const` doesn't make a variable "not stored anywhere" — it tells the compiler (and readers) that this value should never be reassigned after initialization, and the compiler will reject code that tries:

```c
const double PI = 3.14159265358979;
// PI = 4.0;  // compile error: assignment of read-only variable
```

Marking values `const` wherever they don't change is cheap, catches accidental mutation, and documents intent for the next reader.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Implicit `int` (legacy C).** Old C (pre-C99) allowed omitting a return type or variable type, silently defaulting to `int`. Modern compilers warn or error on this — always write explicit types and return types.
- **Integer overflow.** Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior in C (not a wraparound you can rely on): `INT_MAX + 1` does not reliably give you `INT_MIN`. Use wider types (`long long`) or `<stdint.h>` unsigned types (which *do* wrap predictably, modulo 2^n) when a value might exceed `int`'s range.
- **Mismatched `printf`/`scanf` specifiers.** `%d` for a `long`, or `%f` where a `double*` was expected by `scanf`, is undefined behavior — the compiler often warns (`-Wformat`), but nothing stops it at runtime.
- **Comparing signed and unsigned.** `if (someInt < someUnsigned)` triggers an implicit conversion of the signed value to unsigned, which can silently turn negative numbers into huge positive ones. Watch for `size_t` comparisons against possibly-negative `int`s.
- **`sizeof` on a pointer vs. an array.** `sizeof(arr)` on a real array gives the *whole array's* byte size; the moment that array decays to a pointer (e.g. passed to a function), `sizeof` on the parameter gives the *pointer's* size instead — a frequent source of confusion covered in more depth in the arrays module.

Writing clean, explicit, initialized, well-typed C from the start avoids the majority of bugs beginners hit with this module's material.

modules.title: Operators, Expressions & Type Conversion

pages.title: Operators and Expressions
pages.markdown:
## The Operator Families

C's operators are the template every later C-family language (C++, Java, JavaScript, C#) copied almost verbatim:

- **Arithmetic**: `+ - * / %` (modulo only applies to integers)
- **Relational**: `< <= > >= == !=`
- **Logical**: `&& || !` (operate on "truthiness": 0 is false, nonzero is true)
- **Bitwise**: `& | ^ ~ << >>` (operate on the raw bits of integers)
- **Assignment**: `= += -= *= /= %= &= |= ^= <<= >>=`
- **Increment/decrement**: `++` and `--`, both prefix (`++x`) and postfix (`x++`)

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int a = 7, b = 2;
    printf("%d\n", a + b);   // 9
    printf("%d\n", a % b);   // 1
    printf("%d\n", a << 1);  // 14 (bit-shift left = multiply by 2)
    printf("%d\n", a & b);   // 2  (bitwise AND)
    return 0;
}
```

## Integer Division Truncates

`/` between two integers discards any fractional part rather than rounding:

```c
int a = 7, b = 2;
printf("%d\n", a / b);              // 3, not 3.5
printf("%f\n", (double)a / b);      // 3.500000
```

Casting **one** operand to `double` before the division forces the whole expression to compute in floating point — the classic fix for "integer division gave me the wrong answer."

## No Built-In `bool` (Classically)

Pre-C99, C has no boolean type: any nonzero value is "true" in a condition, and `0` is "false." Comparisons like `a == b` produce an `int` (`1` or `0`), not a distinct boolean type.

```c
int flag = 5;
if (flag) printf("nonzero is true\n"); // runs — 5 is truthy
```

C99 added `<stdbool.h>`, which supplies `bool`, `true`, and `false` as macros layered over `int` (`bool` is `_Bool` under the hood, `true` is `1`, `false` is `0`) — mostly for readability, not a fundamentally new type.

## Operator Precedence

Like arithmetic in school, `*` and `/` bind tighter than `+` and `-`, and comparisons bind looser than arithmetic but tighter than `&&`/`||`. When in doubt, **use parentheses** — precedence bugs (`a & b == c`, where `==` actually binds tighter than `&`, surprising many people) are a real and common source of defects. Explicit parentheses cost nothing and remove all ambiguity for the reader.

pages.title: Type Conversion & Evaluation Order Nuances
pages.markdown:
## Implicit Conversions: the "Usual Arithmetic Conversions"

When an expression mixes types, C converts operands following a fixed ranking (roughly: `char`/`short` promote to `int`; then if types still differ, the "smaller" or signed one converts toward the "larger" or unsigned one). Mixing `int` and `double` promotes the `int` to `double` before the operation:

```c
int a = 7;
double b = 2.0;
double result = a / b; // a promoted to 7.0 first, result is 3.5
```

## Explicit Casts

`(Type)expr` forces a conversion regardless of the implicit rules:

```c
double d = 9.7;
int i = (int)d;   // 9 — truncates toward zero, does not round
```

Casting `double` to `int` **truncates** (discards the fractional part) rather than rounding — `(int)9.7` is `9`, and `(int)-9.7` is `-9` (toward zero, not toward negative infinity). Use `round()` from `<math.h>` if you actually want rounding.

## The Signed/Unsigned Trap

When a signed and an unsigned integer of the same rank are compared or combined, the signed value is converted to unsigned — a negative number becomes a huge positive one:

```c
int a = -1;
unsigned int b = 1;
if (a < b) printf("a is smaller\n");  // does NOT print!
```

Here `a` converts to `UINT_MAX` (the largest unsigned value) before comparison, so `a < b` is false. This is a genuine, frequently-hit bug source whenever `size_t` (unsigned) is compared against a plain, possibly-negative `int`.

## Sequence Points and Undefined Behavior

C does not guarantee left-to-right evaluation order for most operators, including function arguments and most binary operators. Modifying the same variable more than once between "sequence points" without an intervening one is undefined behavior:

```c
int i = 0;
int arr[3] = {0};
arr[i] = i++;       // undefined behavior — order of the write and the increment is unspecified
printf("%d %d\n", i++, i++); // undefined behavior — same variable modified twice, order unspecified
```

Write these as separate statements instead:

```c
arr[i] = i;
i++;
```

## Short-Circuit Evaluation

`&&` and `||` **do** guarantee left-to-right evaluation, and stop as soon as the result is determined — the right-hand side is not evaluated if the left side already decides it. This is relied on constantly to guard against invalid operations:

```c
if (ptr != NULL && ptr->value > 0) { /* safe: ptr->value only
                                          evaluated if ptr isn't NULL */ }
```

If `&&` did not short-circuit, this pattern would dereference a null pointer whenever `ptr` was `NULL`.

pages.title: Idioms & Common Pitfalls
pages.markdown:
## The Ternary Operator

`condition ? a : b` is a compact expression-level if/else, useful for simple value selection:

```c
int a = 7, b = 3;
int max = (a > b) ? a : b;
```

Avoid nesting more than one level deep — chained ternaries quickly become unreadable compared to a plain `if/else`.

## Bit Manipulation Idioms

Bitwise operators are heavily used for flags, masks, and low-level protocol/hardware work:

```c
#define FLAG_READ   (1 << 0)  // 0b001
#define FLAG_WRITE  (1 << 1)  // 0b010
#define FLAG_EXEC   (1 << 2)  // 0b100

unsigned int perms = FLAG_READ | FLAG_WRITE; // set bits
int canWrite = perms & FLAG_WRITE;           // test a bit
perms &= ~FLAG_WRITE;                        // clear a bit
perms ^= FLAG_EXEC;                          // toggle a bit
```

This "set / test / clear / toggle" idiom is everywhere in embedded and systems C — status registers, permission flags, protocol headers.

## Avoid Multiple Side Effects in One Expression

Because evaluation order for most operators is unspecified, never rely on a specific order between two increments/decrements/assignments of the *same* variable in one expression. When it's not obvious an expression is safe, split it into separate statements — the compiler can still optimize it just as well, and the reader (and you, in six months) will thank you.

## Comparing Floating Point Safely

Never write `if (x == y)` for floats/doubles derived from computation. Use a tolerance (an "epsilon"):

```c
#include <math.h>
if (fabs(x - y) < 1e-9) { /* considered equal */ }
```

## Watch Signed/Unsigned Mixing

Prefer keeping a consistent signedness within a comparison. If you must compare a `size_t` (from `strlen`, `sizeof`, array indices) against something that might be negative, cast deliberately and comment why:

```c
long diff = -1;
size_t len = 5;
if (diff < 0 || (size_t)diff < len) { /* handle safely */ }
```

## `<stdbool.h>` for Readability

Modern idiomatic C99+ uses `bool` for functions/variables that are conceptually true/false, even though it's just `int` underneath — it documents intent clearly to readers:

```c
#include <stdbool.h>

bool isEven(int n) {
    return n % 2 == 0;
}
```

modules.title: Input & Output

pages.title: printf and scanf Basics
Buffering & the Mechanics of Stream Parsing
pages.markdown:
## Buffered I/O

Streams in C are typically **buffered**: output doesn't necessarily reach the terminal or file the instant you call `printf` — it accumulates in an internal buffer that's flushed when it fills up, when the program exits normally, or when you flush it explicitly with `fflush(stdout)`. `stdout` is usually **line-buffered** when connected to a terminal (flushes on `\n`) but **fully buffered** when redirected to a file or pipe (flushes only when the buffer is full) — a subtlety that can make output appear "out of order" relative to `stderr`, which is unbuffered.

```c
printf("processing...");   // may not appear immediately if stdout isn't line-buffered
fflush(stdout);             // force it out now
```

## How `scanf` Actually Parses

`scanf`'s format specifiers skip leading whitespace **except** `%c`, which reads the very next character — including a stray newline left over from a previous `%d` or `%s` read. This is the single most common `scanf` gotcha:

```c
int n;
char c;
scanf("%d", &n);   // user types "5\n" — scanf consumes "5", leaves "\n" in the buffer
scanf(" %c", &c);  // the leading space here skips that leftover "\n"
```

Without the leading space in `" %c"`, `c` would silently be assigned the newline character rather than the character the user intended to type next.

## `%s` Reads a "Word," Not a Line

`scanf("%s", buf)` reads characters up to (but not including) the next whitespace — it does **not** read a full line, and it has **no idea how big `buf` is**, so it will happily write past the end of an undersized buffer (a classic buffer overflow). This is why `scanf("%s", ...)` on raw user input is considered unsafe in production code without a width limit (`scanf("%31s", buf)` for a 32-byte buffer).

## `EOF` and Loop Termination

`scanf` (and `getchar`) return the constant `EOF` when the input stream ends (e.g. piped input runs out, or the user sends Ctrl-D/Ctrl-Z). A common pattern reads until input is exhausted or invalid:

```c
int n, total = 0;
while (scanf("%d", &n) == 1) {
    total += n;
}
printf("total = %d\n", total);
```

This loop cleanly stops on either malformed input or end-of-stream, since both cause `scanf` to return something other than `1`.

modules.title: Arrays, Strings & String Manipulation

pages.title: Arrays and C-Strings
Pointer Arithmetic & Memory Layout
pages.markdown:
## Array-to-Pointer Decay

Whenever an array is used in most expressions (passed to a function, assigned to a pointer, etc.), it **decays** to a pointer to its first element — the array "loses" its size information at that point:

```c
int nums[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
int *p = nums;          // p now points at nums[0]; decay happened here
printf("%d\n", *p);      // 1
printf("%d\n", *(p + 2)); // 3 — same as nums[2]
```

`sizeof(nums)` (the original array, still known to be an array by the compiler at that point) gives `20` (5 ints × 4 bytes); `sizeof(p)` gives the size of a pointer (commonly 8 on 64-bit systems) — a frequent point of confusion once decay has happened, e.g. across a function call boundary.

## Pointer Arithmetic Is Scaled

`p + 1` doesn't advance one byte — it advances by `sizeof(*p)` bytes, i.e., one whole element:

```c
char *cp = "abc";
int  *ip = (int[]){10, 20, 30};
printf("%p vs %p\n", (void*)cp, (void*)(cp + 1)); // advances by 1 byte
printf("%p vs %p\n", (void*)ip, (void*)(ip + 1)); // advances by 4 bytes (sizeof(int))
```

This scaling is exactly why `arr[i]` == `*(arr + i)` produces the correct element regardless of the element's size.

## Multi-Dimensional Arrays Are Row-Major, Contiguous

A 2D array like `int grid[3][4]` is a single contiguous block of 12 `int`s, laid out row by row ("row-major"). `grid[r][c]` computes to `*(*(grid + r) + c)`:

```c
int grid[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};
printf("%d\n", grid[1][2]); // 6 — the 6th int in memory order
```

Passing a 2D array to a function requires specifying every dimension except the first (`void f(int grid[][3])`), because the compiler needs the row width to compute offsets correctly.

## String Literals Live in Read-Only Memory

A string literal like `"hello"` is typically stored in a read-only data segment. A `char*` pointing at one must never be written through:

```c
char *s = "hello";
s[0] = 'H'; // undefined behavior — often a crash (segfault) on modern systems

char arr[] = "hello"; // this copies into a mutable, stack-allocated array
arr[0] = 'H';          // fine — arr is a real, writable array
```

The distinction — `char *s = "literal"` (pointer to read-only data) vs. `char arr[] = "literal"` (a fresh, mutable, stack-allocated copy) — is one of the most important nuances in this module.

keyTakeaways: C has no try/catch — functions signal failure via return value (NULL, -1, an error enum, etc.).
errno is set by many standard functions on failure; check it immediately after, and use strerror()/perror() to decode it.
errno is guaranteed thread-local since C11, and is not automatically cleared on success — only trust it right after a failing call.
The caller is responsible for checking every fallible return value; nothing in the language enforces this.
assert() catches programmer bugs/invariant violations and is typically compiled out in release builds — never use it to validate user input.
exit() runs atexit()-registered handlers; prefer EXIT_SUCCESS/EXIT_FAILURE over raw 0/1 for portability.
The goto cleanup idiom centralizes resource release across multiple failure points in one function, since C has no finally block.
setjmp/longjmp allow non-local jumps up the call stack but skip any cleanup in the frames jumped over.

modules.title: Pointers & Manual Memory Management

pages.title: Pointer Fundamentals
Heap Allocation Mechanics & Memory Layout
Idioms & Memory-Safety Pitfalls
pages.markdown:
## Always Check Allocation Return Values

`malloc`/`calloc`/`realloc` can fail (return `NULL`) when memory is exhausted. Idiomatic C checks every allocation before using it:

```c
int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
if (arr == NULL) {
    fprintf(stderr, "out of memory\n");
    return -1;
}
```

## Null Out Pointers After Freeing

Setting a pointer to `NULL` immediately after `free`ing it turns any accidental later use into an immediate, loud, easy-to-diagnose `NULL`-dereference crash instead of subtle dangling-pointer corruption:

```c
free(p);
p = NULL; // any accidental *p or p->field after this crashes cleanly, instead of corrupting memory
```

## Avoid Double-Free

Calling `free` twice on the same pointer is undefined behavior (it typically corrupts the allocator's internal bookkeeping) — the `p = NULL` idiom above also helps here, since `free(NULL)` is always a guaranteed-safe no-op:

```c
free(p);
p = NULL;
free(p); // now a harmless no-op, instead of a double-free bug
```

## Ownership Conventions

C has no language-enforced ownership model (unlike Rust), so every API needs a **documented convention** for who is responsible for eventually calling `free()` on a given pointer — "the caller owns the returned pointer and must free it," or "the function takes ownership of the pointer you pass in." Getting this wrong in either direction causes either a leak (nobody frees it) or a double-free (two owners both think they should).

## One `malloc`, One `free` — Match Every Allocation

The cardinal rule of manual memory management: every successful allocation needs exactly one corresponding `free`, on every code path, including error paths — which is exactly what the `goto cleanup` idiom (error-handling module) exists to guarantee even when a function has several possible early-return points.

## Tools That Catch These Bugs For You

Memory bugs are notoriously hard to spot by inspection alone. Real-world C development leans heavily on tools:

- **Valgrind** (`valgrind ./program`) — detects leaks, use-after-free, and invalid reads/writes at runtime.
- **AddressSanitizer** (`-fsanitize=address` when compiling with gcc/clang) — instruments the binary to catch memory errors immediately, with much lower overhead than Valgrind.

Using one of these routinely, especially in tests, catches the majority of memory bugs long before they reach production.

## Pointer Arithmetic Stays Within Bounds

Never compute a pointer more than one-past-the-end of its array/allocation, and never dereference a pointer that's exactly one-past-the-end:

```c
int arr[5];
int *end = arr + 5;   // legal to compute (one-past-the-end), but...
int bad = *end;        // ...dereferencing it is undefined behavior
```

codeExamples.explanation: Uses a temporary pointer to hold realloc's result, avoiding a leak if realloc fails and returns NULL.

keyTakeaways: & takes an address; * dereferences a pointer to read/write the pointee.
malloc/calloc allocate heap memory; every successful allocation must be matched by exactly one free().
There is no garbage collector — you are fully responsible for memory lifetime across every code path.
realloc may move the block and return NULL on failure without freeing the original — assign to a temporary pointer first.
Use-after-free, double-free, and buffer overruns are undefined behavior and common serious bug sources.
Null out a pointer immediately after freeing it, and free(NULL) is always guaranteed to be a safe no-op.
Pointer arithmetic is only well-defined within (or one-past-the-end of) a single allocation or array.
Valgrind and AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address) are standard tools for catching memory bugs during development.

modules.title: File I/O & Standard Library / Header Highlights

pages.title: File I/O Basics
Buffering, the Preprocessor, and Header Mechanics
pages.markdown:
## Checking for Errors and End-of-File

`feof(f)` and `ferror(f)` distinguish *why* a read stopped short — reaching the end of the file is not an error, but a genuine I/O failure is:

```c
size_t got = fread(buf, 1, sizeof(buf), f);
if (got < sizeof(buf)) {
    if (feof(f)) {
        printf("reached end of file\n");
    } else if (ferror(f)) {
        printf("a read error occurred\n");
    }
}
```

Relying purely on a read returning fewer bytes than requested, without checking which of these caused it, is a common subtle bug.

## Buffering and `fflush`

Like `stdout`, file streams are buffered by default — writes may sit in memory until the buffer fills, the file is closed, or you call `fflush(f)` explicitly. This matters when another process might read the file concurrently, or when a crash could lose unflushed data:

```c
fprintf(f, "critical log line\n");
fflush(f); // ensure it's actually on disk now, not just buffered in memory
```

## The Preprocessor Runs Before the Compiler

Introduced in module 1, the preprocessor is a distinct text-substitution pass. Its major directives:

- `#include` — paste in another file's contents (a header, typically).
- `#define NAME value` — a simple text-substitution macro.
- `#define NAME(args) expr` — a **function-like macro**, substituted with its arguments textually.
- `#ifdef`/`#ifndef`/`#endif` — conditional compilation, include or exclude code based on whether a name is defined.

```c
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
#define MAX_USERS 100

#ifdef DEBUG
    #define LOG(msg) printf("[DEBUG] %s\n", msg)
#else
    #define LOG(msg) /* nothing — compiled away entirely */
#endif
```

Because macros are pasted in *before* the compiler ever parses C syntax or types, they have no notion of scope, type-checking, or namespaces — they're pure text substitution, which is both their power and their danger (elaborated on the next page).

## Include Guards Prevent Double-Inclusion

If two different headers both `#include "utils.h"`, and a third file includes both of them, `utils.h`'s contents would be pasted in **twice** — usually a compile error from duplicate type/function definitions. **Include guards** prevent this:

```c
/* utils.h */
#ifndef UTILS_H
#define UTILS_H

int square(int n);
#define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))

#endif /* UTILS_H */
```

The first time `utils.h` is included, `UTILS_H` isn't yet defined, so its contents are processed (and `UTILS_H` gets defined). Any subsequent `#include "utils.h"` in the same translation unit sees `UTILS_H` already defined and skips straight to `#endif`, emitting nothing. Many compilers also support `#pragma once` as a non-standard but widely supported shorthand for the same guarantee.

## Declaration vs. Definition Across Files

A header should contain **declarations** (function prototypes, `extern` variable declarations, type definitions) — never a function's actual body or a non-`extern` global variable, or every `.c` file that includes it would define the same symbol, causing a "multiple definition" linker error. Actual definitions belong in exactly one `.c` file.

pages.title: Macro Idioms & Common Pitfalls
pages.markdown:
## Always Parenthesize Macro Parameters (and the Whole Expansion)

Because macros are pure text substitution, forgetting parentheses causes the substituted expression to combine unexpectedly with surrounding code due to operator precedence:

```c
#define SQUARE(x) x * x

int result = 100 / SQUARE(2);
/* expands to: 100 / 2 * 2 = 100, not 100 / 4 = 25 as intended! */
```

The fix is to parenthesize both each parameter's use *and* the overall expansion:

```c
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))

int result = 100 / SQUARE(2); // now correctly 100 / (2 * 2) = 25
```

## Macros Can Evaluate Arguments Multiple Times

A macro parameter used more than once in its expansion re-evaluates whatever expression was passed — dangerous if that expression has **side effects**:

```c
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))

int i = 5;
int result = SQUARE(i++); // expands to ((i++) * (i++)) — undefined behavior!
```

This is a genuine advantage real functions have over macros: a function's arguments are evaluated exactly once, always. When a computed value might have side effects, prefer an actual (possibly `inline`) function over a macro.

## `inline` Functions Are Often the Better Choice

C99 added `inline` as a hint to the compiler that a small function is a good candidate for inlining at the call site (avoiding call overhead) while still behaving like a real, type-checked function with single evaluation of its arguments — frequently a strictly safer replacement for a computational macro:

```c
static inline int square(int x) { return x * x; }
```

Reach for macros mainly for things functions genuinely cannot do — textual code generation, conditional compilation (`#ifdef`), or stringification (`#x`)/token-pasting (`x##y`) — not as a substitute for small functions.

## `#define` Constants vs. `const`/`enum`

`#define MAX_USERS 100` has no type and is invisible to the debugger (it's gone by the time the compiler sees the code) and to the type system. Modern idiomatic C often prefers `const int MAX_USERS = 100;` (has a real type, visible in a debugger) or an `enum` for a related group of integer constants, reserving `#define` for things that genuinely must be pure text (conditional compilation, header guards).

## X-Macros: a Legitimate Advanced Idiom

One place macros do something genuinely hard to replicate otherwise is generating repetitive, parallel code from one list, the "X-macro" pattern:

```c
#define COLOR_LIST \
    X(RED) \
    X(GREEN) \
    X(BLUE)

typedef enum {
#define X(name) COLOR_##name,
    COLOR_LIST
#undef X
} Color;

const char *colorName(Color c) {
    switch (c) {
#define X(name) case COLOR_##name: return #name;
        COLOR_LIST
#undef X
        default: return "UNKNOWN";
    }
}
```

This generates both the `enum` and its name-lookup function from a single authoritative list — genuinely useful for keeping two things in sync, though it's an advanced, somewhat niche technique most codebases use sparingly.

keyTakeaways: fopen/fprintf/fgets/fread/fwrite/fclose form the standard file I/O toolkit.
Always check fopen's return value for NULL before using the file handle.
feof/ferror distinguish 'reached end of file' from 'an actual I/O error occurred' after a short read.
#define macros are textually substituted by the preprocessor before compilation, with no type-checking or scope.
Include guards (#ifndef/#define/#endif or #pragma once) stop a header's contents from being pasted in more than once.
Headers should contain only declarations; put actual definitions in exactly one .c file to avoid linker errors.
Always parenthesize macro parameters and the overall expansion to avoid operator-precedence bugs.
math.h functions typically require linking the math library (-lm) on Linux; prefer inline functions over macros when arguments may have side effects.
